name: Revolutions of 1848
info: The revolutions of 1848, also called the springtime of the peoples, were a wave of uprisings across Europe from January 1848 to October 1849 against absolute monarchy and feudalism, most of them suppressed within a year or two.

facts.where: Europe, above all France, the Italian states, the Austrian Empire (including Hungary and the Czech lands) and the states of the German Confederation; smaller risings in Denmark, Switzerland, the Romanian Principalities and Ireland; echoes in Latin America and the Dutch East Indies
facts.period: revolution in Sicily January 1848; February Revolution in France and the March risings in Germany, Austria, Hungary and Italy; counter-revolution from May to December 1848; a second wave in 1849 ending with Hungary's surrender in August and the fall of Komárom in October 1849
facts.figures: Louis Philippe I, the French king who abdicated; Klemens von Metternich, Austrian chancellor, who resigned; Lajos Kossuth, leader of the Hungarian government; Giuseppe Mazzini, organiser of Young Italy; Frederick William IV of Prussia, who refused the imperial crown; Louis Napoléon Bonaparte, elected French president in December 1848
facts.outcome: most revolutions were suppressed, tens of thousands were killed and more went into exile; lasting reforms included the end of serfdom in Austria and Hungary, the end of absolute monarchy in Denmark and representative democracy in the Netherlands

t: More than fifty countries were affected by the wave of revolutions between January 1848 and October 1849, but without significant coordination or cooperation among their revolutionaries.

Coalitions of workers and reformers, including members of the middle and upper classes, won early concessions in the spring of 1848, then divided; conservative forces and armies suppressed most of the revolutions, killing tens of thousands of people.
Many of the revolutionaries' goals were achieved within about two decades, largely by their opponents: serfdom ended in Austria and Hungary, and Hungary gained more self-determination in 1867.
dyk: When news of the revolution in France reached Vienna, the Austrian chancellor Klemens von Metternich is said to have exclaimed, in French, "well, my dear, it's all over!"; a few weeks later he resigned and went into exile.
ev: A revolution in Palermo, Sicily, begins the wave of revolutions in January
King Louis Philippe I abdicates on 24 February and the French Second Republic is proclaimed
Fighting in Vienna in March forces Metternich to resign, and barricade fighting in Berlin leads Frederick William IV to withdraw the army
The June Days uprising of Paris workers is suppressed by General Cavaignac, and Louis Napoléon Bonaparte is elected French president in December
King Frederick William IV of Prussia rejects the imperial crown offered by the Frankfurt National Assembly
The Roman Republic falls to French intervention in July and Venice surrenders in August
Hungary surrenders to Austria and Russia on 13 August, and the fortress of Komárom falls in October

sections.background:
The revolutions grew out of the short- and long-term changes brought by industrialisation and out of the political legacy of the French Revolution: rapid population growth, urbanisation, a repressive political order set up in reaction to the French Revolution, and the spread of liberalism, radicalism and nationalism. In the countryside peasants had lost customary rights to common land and forests through enclosure and privatisation; in the Bavarian Palatinate those convicted of wood theft rose from 37,500 in 1821–22 to 185,000 in 1846–47. The largest pre-revolutionary peasant uprising against feudal lords took place in Austrian Galicia in 1846.

Urban workers met oversupplied labour markets and falling real wages. Most workers in 1848 were skilled artisans, whom mechanisation threatened. Educated men found too few careers: Wilhelm Heinrich Riehl wrote of an "intellectual proletariat" in Germany, and many who failed in their professions turned to journalism and later led the revolutions.

According to the economic historians Helge Berger and Mark Spoerer, the most immediate cause was the economic crisis of 1845 to 1847. Potato blight devastated harvests from 1845, and the Great Famine directly killed over an eighth of Ireland's population, over 1 million of 8 million. Food riots followed, over 400 in France in 1846–47 and 164 in the German states in 1847, and an industrial recession came in 1847. Berger and Spoerer found a strong correlation between the countries most deeply hit by it and those that had a revolution in 1848.
sections.aims:
The revolutions varied widely in their aims but generally opposed conservative systems such as absolute monarchy and feudalism and sought nation states founded on constitutionalism and popular sovereignty. Three currents opposed the governments. Liberals supported equality before the law, civil liberties including the right to own property, and constitutions; they preferred constitutional monarchy to absolute monarchy or radical republic, and generally sought a franchise restricted to male property-owners. Radicals, a loose coalition of democrats and socialists, wanted universal manhood suffrage and gave greater weight to the "social question" of the working poor. Radical democrats generally favoured regulation and state intervention, while socialists sought the abolition of capitalism.

Nationalism promoted the unity and primacy of people bound by common language, culture, religion, history and geography. Workers demanded the right of association: in France through cooperatives, mutual benefit societies and early trade unions, in Germany partly through a return to the guild system.

Reformers across Europe demanded a representative parliament, freedom of the press, freedom of association, universal manhood suffrage and a national guard. The Hungarian 12 points of 15 March 1848 added an independent Hungarian ministry, trial by jury, a Hungarian army, civil and religious equality and union with Transylvania. In Wallachia the Proclamation of Islaz announced reforms including autonomy and the abolition of serfdom.
sections.events:
A revolution in Palermo in January 1848 began the wave, but the revolution in France in February held far greater import among contemporaries. After protests in Paris on 22 February and the army's massacre of 65 demonstrators on 23 February, Louis Philippe I abdicated on 24 February. Within weeks there were uprisings in Munich, Vienna, Buda and Pest, Venice, Kraków, Milan and Berlin. Governments mostly capitulated without significant resistance: Metternich resigned after violent clashes in Vienna from 13 to 15 March, and in Berlin, after barricade fighting on 18 March, Frederick William IV ordered the army to withdraw. Elections under broad franchises followed, including to the Frankfurt National Assembly.

Divisions soon appeared. In France the Constituent Assembly elected on 23 April had a conservative majority, and the closing of the national workshops on 21 June led to the June Days uprising, in which 40,000 to 50,000 insurgents fought on the barricades of Paris until General Cavaignac suppressed it with significant bloodshed. Habsburg forces bombarded Prague in June, Radetzky defeated the Piedmontese at Custoza in July, and Jelačić and Windisch-Grätz crushed the Vienna Uprising on 31 October.

In 1849 Piedmont–Sardinia was beaten again at Novara in March. Frederick William IV rejected the Frankfurt crown, and the Imperial Constitution campaign in Germany ended in defeat in July. The Roman Republic fell in July and Venice surrendered in August. Hungary, invaded by Russia, surrendered on 13 August, and the last holdouts at Komárom gave in between 2 and 5 October.
sections.people:
In France Louis Philippe I was the king who abdicated, Louis Blanc, a socialist in the provisional government, led the Luxembourg Commission, and General Louis-Eugène Cavaignac suppressed the June Days. Louis Napoléon Bonaparte, nephew of Napoleon, won the presidential election of 10 December 1848 with 75 percent of the vote, with conservatives, peasants and urban workers backing him for different reasons; in December 1851 he launched a coup d'état, and the following year he took the name Napoleon III.

Giuseppe Mazzini led the Young Italy movement within the larger Young Europe network, whose methods contemporaries widely admired and imitated. In the Habsburg lands Metternich resigned and went into exile, Ferdinand I abdicated in December 1848 in favour of Franz Joseph I, and Lajos Kossuth led the Hungarian government. Sándor Petőfi's poetry was read aloud with the 12 points in Pest. František Palacký propagated Austroslavism, which sought greater autonomy for the Czech lands within the monarchy.

In Germany Friedrich Hecker and Gustav Struve led a radical republican uprising in Baden in April 1848, Archduke John of Austria served as Imperial Regent, and Robert Blum was executed by Austrian troops. Frederick William IV of Prussia refused the crown. Karl Marx was expelled from Brussels in early March 1848 on accusations of having helped arm Belgian revolutionaries.
sections.outcomes:
Many of the revolutions were quickly suppressed, tens of thousands of people were killed and even more were forced into exile. By the end of 1848 decidedly conservative governments had come to power across Europe: Frederick William IV dismissed his liberal ministers and imposed a conservative constitution, and Franz Joseph I's government dissolved the Reichstag in March 1849 and issued the March Constitution. In Hungary, the leading rebels such as Kossuth went into exile or were executed, among them former prime minister Batthyány and the Thirteen Martyrs of Arad. Governments partly reversed the reforms; arrests in Habsburg territories rose from 70,000 in 1850 to one million by 1854, and censorship tightened in Russia.

Some reforms lasted. Serfdom was abolished in the Austrian Empire by a patent of 7 September 1848, absolute monarchy ended in Denmark, and the Netherlands and Switzerland altered their constitutions. Tensions between bourgeois revolutionaries and radicals played a major role in the failure of the revolutions, and national conflicts, among Germans, Poles, Danes, Czechs, Magyars, Croats and Romanians, divided the revolutionaries.

Many historians long considered the revolutions a failure, given the lack of visible structural change after 1848. Christopher Clark characterises the following period as one dominated by a revolution in government, as states managed the public sphere more effectively. Priscilla Robertson considered many of the revolutionaries' goals achieved by the 1870s, though largely by the enemies of the revolutions.
sections.legacy:
Interpretations differ. Liberal democrats looked to 1848 as a democratic revolution that in the long run ensured liberty, equality and fraternity. For nationalists it was the springtime of hope, though the results fell short of what many had hoped. Communists denounced it as a betrayal of working-class ideals by an indifferent bourgeoisie, and the view of 1848 as a bourgeois revolution is also common in non-Marxist scholarship. Karl Marx expressed disappointment at its bourgeois character and in 1850 set out a theory of permanent revolution.

After the revolutions Russia abolished serfdom in 1861, France kept the universal male suffrage the Second Republic had set up, and the Austrian Empire was reorganised into the Dual Monarchy through the Ausgleich of 1867, spearheaded by the former revolutionaries Gyula Andrássy and Ferenc Deák. In Piedmont–Sardinia centrist coalitions such as Cavour's Connubio took power.

Disillusioned and persecuted revolutionaries, above all from Germany and the Austrian Empire, went into exile and became known as the Forty-Eighters. About 4,000 went to the United States, including Carl Schurz; German American sentiment was largely anti-slavery, especially among the Forty-Eighters. The German historian Reinhard Rürup described the revolutions as a turning point in the development of modern antisemitism, as conspiracy theories presented Jews as representing both social revolution and international capital.

summary: The revolutions of 1848 were a wave of uprisings across Europe between January 1848 and October 1849 against absolute monarchy and feudalism. Coalitions of workers and reformers won early concessions but soon divided, and most revolutions were suppressed, though serfdom ended in Austria and Hungary.
references: Christopher Clark, Revolutionary Spring: Europe Aflame and the Fight for a New World, 1848-1849 (Crown Publishing, 2023)
Mike Rapport, 1848: Year of Revolution (Basic Books, 2009)
Priscilla Robertson, Revolutions of 1848: A Social History (Princeton University Press, 1971)
Jonathan Sperber, The European Revolutions, 1848–1851 (Cambridge University Press, 2005)
Peter N. Stearns, 1848: The Revolutionary Tide in Europe (W. W. Norton & Company, 1974)
notes: Region: the article also covers Latin America, Canada, the United States and the Dutch East Indies; the profile keeps to Europe as given.
Russian force in Hungary: the Chronology says Russia mobilised 200,000 troops, the Hungary section says Nicholas I marched in with over 300,000. I gave neither figure.
Prague: the Chronology calls it the June Uprising provoked by Windisch-Grätz; written as the bombardment of Prague in June.
Dates of end: the lede says January 1848 to October 1849; Komárom surrendered 2 to 5 October 1849. Hungary's capitulation is 13 August.

Kingdom of the Two Sicilies: the Sicilian state lasted 16 months, left out for length. Switzerland's Sonderbund war (about 100 killed, 1847) and the 1848 constitution, Belgium, Ireland (Young Ireland), the Romanian principalities, Denmark's constitution and Schleswig, and Latin America are covered in the article but mostly omitted for length.
The 1851 coup and 1852 empire in France are said by the article to end the revolution there; included in the people section.
Wording check: 'Thirteen Martyrs of Arad' and 'Batthyány' appear in the article without a first name; kept as given.

Left out: the Hanoverian and Prussian noble recoveries of privileges, popular culture items, and Metternich-style quotations other than the one in dyk. The dyk's 'a few weeks later he resigned' is from the article (resigned after the clashes of 13 to 15 March).
